Introduction to Anatomical Terms & Body Organisation

The language of anatomy — positions, planes, movement terms and how the body is organised from cell to system.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Use correct anatomical terms for position and movement
  • Name the planes and body cavities
  • List the levels of body organisation

In simple words

Anatomy needs a fixed starting position so that “above” and “left” mean the same thing to everyone. That position is the anatomical position: standing upright, face forward, arms by the side, palms facing forward, feet together.

From that position we describe the body using planes, directions and movement words. Learn these first — every later chapter uses them.

Key points

Levels of organisation: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.

Four tissue types: epithelial (covering), connective (support), muscular (movement), nervous (control).

Term Meaning
Anterior / ventral Towards the front
Posterior / dorsal Towards the back
Superior Towards the head
Inferior Towards the feet
Medial Towards the midline
Lateral Away from the midline
Proximal Nearer the trunk
Distal Farther from the trunk
Superficial Near the surface
Deep Away from the surface
Supine Lying on the back
Prone Lying on the face

Planes

  • Sagittal — divides left and right.
  • Coronal (frontal) — divides front and back.
  • Transverse (horizontal) — divides upper and lower.

Movements: flexion (bending), extension (straightening), abduction (away from midline), adduction (towards midline), rotation, circumduction, supination (palm up), pronation (palm down), inversion/eversion (sole in/out), dorsiflexion/plantar flexion (foot up/down).

Body cavities: cranial (brain), vertebral (spinal cord), thoracic (heart, lungs), abdominal (gut, liver, spleen, kidneys), pelvic (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs). The diaphragm separates thoracic from abdominal.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Anatomical position: standing, face forward, arms by the side, palms forward.
  2. Three planes: sagittal (left/right), coronal (front/back), transverse (upper/lower).
  3. Levels of organisation: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
  4. Supine = on the back; prone = on the face.
  5. Diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Proximal/distal are used for limbs; superior/inferior for the trunk and head.
  2. Four tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous.
  3. Abduction moves away from the midline; adduction moves towards it.

Memory trick

Sagittal = “S” for side-to-side split. Coronal = “C” for crown (front/back). Transverse = across.

For proximal/distal think: “PROximal = close to home”.

60-second revision

  • Anatomical position = palms forward, standing.
  • Sagittal / coronal / transverse planes.
  • Medial = midline, lateral = outside.
  • Supine back, prone face down.
  • Four tissue types, five levels of organisation.

Test yourself

A plane that divides the body into equal right and left halves is called:

Answer: B. The sagittal plane divides the body into right and left parts; the midline sagittal plane divides it into equal halves.

The term 'distal' means:

Answer: B. Distal means farther from the point of attachment, for example the fingers are distal to the elbow.

Which cavity contains the heart and lungs?

Answer: C. The thoracic cavity is above the diaphragm and contains the heart, lungs, trachea and oesophagus.

In the anatomical position, the palms face:

Answer: B. In the anatomical position the body stands upright, face forward, arms by the side and palms facing forward.

Abduction of the arm means:

Answer: B. Abduction is movement away from the midline; adduction is movement towards it.

Which plane divides the body into upper and lower parts?

Answer: C. The transverse (horizontal) plane divides the body into upper and lower parts.
